content.title: About
content.content: Fruit scones are soft, lightly sweet British biscuits that incorporate pieces of fresh or dried fruit (such as raisins, cranberries, or blueberries) into the dough. They are commonly served with tea or coffee and can be either mildly sweet or slightly tart depending on the fruit used.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Scones originated in Scotland in the 19th century and quickly became popular throughout England.
Traditional scones are leavened with baking powder rather than yeast, giving them a denser texture than cupcakes.
Fruit scones are often finished with a dusting of powdered sugar or a light glaze.
In the United States the closest counterpart is the muffin, though scones are usually less sweet and more crumbly.
Scones are traditionally served with clotted cream and jam.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: The fruit adds dietary fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Whole‑grain flour provides B1, B2, and niacin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Berries and dried fruits are rich in antioxidants such as vitamin C and polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Compared with many baked goods, scones typically contain a modest amount of butter, making them lower in saturated fat.

items.title: Moderate glycemic index
items.content: The combination of whole grains and fruit yields a slower rise in blood sugar than refined white bread.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Traditional scone recipes use wheat flour, which can be problematic for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Fruit additions and occasional added sugar increase the calorie count and may be unsuitable for diabetics.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite modest fat levels, scones are still relatively calorie‑dense due to carbohydrates and butter.

items.title: Dried fruit additives
items.content: Some dried fruits contain added sugars or preservatives; choose unsweetened varieties when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Fruit scones are best served warm, split in half and spread with butter, clotted cream, or jam. They make a convenient snack, a breakfast accompaniment, or a light dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store scones in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 2 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 5 days) or freeze (up to 2 months). Reheat in the oven or toaster before serving.
